10920: A mountebank is a person who deliberately deceives people — usually through a flashy, persuasive performance — in order to gain something, most often money. Think of it as a supercharged, theatrical version of a con artist or a fraud. The word is not just about lying; it specifically captures the image of someone who puts on a show to trick you.

A mountebank has a very specific recipe of traits that sets them apart from a plain, ordinary liar:

  • They make false claims with great confidence. A mountebank doesn't mumble their lies — they announce them boldly, loudly, and with the energy of someone who truly believes what they're saying (or at least wants you to believe they do).
  • They use entertainment and spectacle. A mountebank draws a crowd. They use charm, humor, dramatic gestures, or impressive-sounding words to keep your attention and lower your guard.
  • They present themselves as an expert or authority. They want you to trust them as someone with special knowledge or power.
  • Their goal is personal gain. All the performance is a means to an end — getting your money, your vote, your loyalty, or some other advantage.
  • Their claims are knowingly false. This is important. A mountebank knows they're deceiving you. They are not simply mistaken or misguided — they are deliberately dishonest.

Historically, the word painted a very vivid picture: imagine a traveling salesman standing on a makeshift platform in a crowded marketplace, waving bottles of colored liquid in the air, and shouting that his miraculous potion can cure blindness, arthritis, baldness, and heartbreak — all for just a few coins. He might even have an assistant performing tricks or telling jokes nearby to keep the crowd entertained. People, dazzled by the performance and swept up in the excitement, hand over their money. The potion, of course, is worthless. That man on the platform is the archetypal mountebank.

This image — the raised platform, the spectacle, the fake medicine, the crowd — is the soul of the word. Even when used today in very different situations, that spirit is always present.

Today, you don't need a marketplace or a fake potion to be called a mountebank. The word is used more broadly for anyone whose deception has that same quality of showmanship and bold false claims. You might hear it used to describe:

  • A politician who makes grand, emotional promises they know they cannot keep, purely to win votes.
  • A wellness guru selling useless supplements with dramatic testimonials and celebrity endorsements.
  • A business leader who hypes up a fraudulent company with dazzling presentations to attract investors.
  • Any self-proclaimed "expert" whose expertise is entirely invented.

The word works best when the deception involves some kind of performance or public display. If someone lies quietly in a back room, they might be a fraud or a swindler — but the word "mountebank" fits most naturally when there's an audience being dazzled.

"Mountebank" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong tone of contempt and ridicule. When you call someone a mountebank, you are not just saying they are dishonest — you are also implying that their whole act is embarrassingly transparent to anyone paying attention. There is something faintly absurd about a mountebank. They are frauds, yes, but they are also, in a way, clowns — people performing a ridiculous act that only works because audiences let themselves be swept up in the excitement.

This gives the word a double edge: it condemns the mountebank for being dishonest, but it also implies a certain foolishness in those who fall for the act. Calling someone a mountebank is one of the sharper insults in the English language.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close relatives, but each has its own flavor:

  • Charlatan — The closest synonym. A charlatan also falsely claims expertise they don't have. However, "charlatan" focuses more on the false credentials, while "mountebank" emphasizes the theatrical performance used to deceive.
  • Quack — A specific type of charlatan: someone who falsely claims to have medical skills or remedies. All quacks are charlatans, but not all charlatans are quacks. A mountebank who sells fake medicine could be called a quack too.
  • Con artist / Swindler — These words focus heavily on the act of stealing money through a scheme. A mountebank can certainly swindle people, but the word "mountebank" is really about the character and style of the person, not just the crime.
  • Fraud — A very general word for someone who deceives. "Mountebank" is a more vivid, colorful, and specific word.

The key distinction to remember: a mountebank deceives with flair. The performance is part of the definition.

Here are some examples that show how the word is naturally used:

  • "He was nothing but a mountebank, promising miraculous investment returns while secretly pocketing the money for himself."
  • "The crowd was initially charmed by the mountebank's smooth talk, but his promises soon fell apart."
  • "History remembers him not as the visionary he claimed to be, but as a mountebank who exploited the desperate."
  • "She saw through the mountebank immediately — his confidence was all theater, and his credentials were invented."

A mountebank is a bold, showy, deliberate deceiver — someone who puts on a convincing performance of expertise or authority in order to trick people, typically for personal gain. They are part fraud, part performer, and entirely untrustworthy.
10921:
To mourn means to feel and/or express deep sadness because of a loss — most commonly, the death of someone you loved. It captures both the inner pain you feel inside your heart and the outward expression of that pain, such as weeping, silence, or somber rituals.

Think of it this way: when something or someone precious to you is gone forever, and that absence creates a heavy ache inside you — that feeling, and everything you do because of it, is mourning.

This is important: "mourn" carries two layers at the same time.

1. The feeling (internal): The deep grief and sadness you experience privately, inside yourself.

2. The expression (external): The way that grief comes out — through tears, through quiet reflection, through wearing black at a funeral, through talking about the person you lost.

You can mourn silently without a single tear, or you can mourn loudly and openly. Both are valid. The word covers the entire experience.

While mourning is most commonly associated with the death of a person, you can mourn any significant loss. Here are the main things people mourn:

A person who has died

"She mourned her father for years after he passed away."

A relationship that has ended

"He mourned the friendship that was destroyed by a misunderstanding."

A lost opportunity

"She mourned the career she never got to have."

A time that is gone

"They mourned the carefree days of their childhood."

A place that no longer exists

"The residents mourned the demolition of their old neighborhood."

A version of yourself

"After the accident, he mourned the person he used to be."

The common thread in all of these is: something is gone, it cannot come back, and you feel a deep sadness about that.

"Mourn" is not a casual or light word. It implies a genuine, serious, deep sadness — not just disappointment or mild unhappiness. If you spill your coffee, you don't mourn it. But if your childhood home is torn down, you might truly mourn it.

The sadness in mourning also tends to have a sense of permanence. You mourn things that are truly lost, not things that might come back.
How Mourn Is Different from Similar Words

These words are related, but they are not the same:

Grieve — This focuses almost entirely on the inner emotional pain. It is more private and personal. Mourning has a slightly broader sense that can include social and public expressions of loss (like a funeral). You can think of grieving as what happens inside you, while mourning can include both the inside and the outside.

Lament — To lament is to mourn with strong verbal expression — to cry out, complain, or protest your loss. Lamenting has more of a voice to it. Mourning can be completely silent; lamenting rarely is.

Weep — This specifically means to cry tears. Mourning is much broader — you can mourn without crying a single tear.

Miss — To miss someone is lighter. You can miss a friend who moved to another city, and that friend is perfectly fine. Missing is about absence. Mourning is specifically about a loss that cannot be undone.
Sentences That Show the Word in Action

• "The whole country mourned when the beloved president died."
  • "She sat quietly by the window, mourning the life she had imagined for herself."
  • "They gathered at the church to mourn the young soldier who did not return home."
  • "He mourned the loss of his old dog for a long time."
  • "The artist mourned the paintings destroyed in the fire."

Since you want a complete picture, here are the other forms of the same word:

  • Mourning (noun/gerund) — The process, act, or period of mourning. "She was in mourning for six months." It can also refer to the social customs around death, like wearing dark clothing.
  • Mourner (noun) — A person who mourns, especially one attending a funeral. "The mourners gathered around the grave."
  • Mournful (adjective) — Expressing or feeling sadness and grief. "He had a mournful look in his eyes." "She played a mournful melody on the piano."
  • Mournfully (adverb) — In a mournful way. "She stared mournfully at the empty chair."

If you want to truly feel what this word means: imagine someone you love deeply. Now imagine they are gone — completely and permanently. The hollow, heavy sadness that settles in your chest, the way the world feels a little dimmer, the way you catch yourself thinking of them and then remembering they are no longer there — that is what it is to mourn.

It is one of the most deeply human experiences, and "mourn" is the word that holds all of it.
10922:
Mournful means deeply and heavily sad — the kind of sadness that comes from grief, loss, or longing. It describes something (or someone) that is filled with sorrow and expresses it, either through appearance, sound, or feeling.

The key word here is expresses. Mournful is not just about feeling sad on the inside. It's about sadness that shows — on someone's face, in their voice, in a sound, or even in a place.
What Makes It Different from Just "Sad"

This is important, because "sad" and "mournful" are not the same thing, even though they are related.

"Sad" is a broad, general word. You can be sad about small things — a bad day, a missed bus, a disappointing meal.

"Mournful" is much heavier and more specific. It carries the weight of grief — the kind of deep sadness you feel after a loss, like the death of a loved one, the end of something precious, or a longing for something that is gone and cannot come back. Think of the sadness at a funeral, or the sadness of looking at an old photograph of someone you will never see again. That is the emotional territory of "mournful."

So every mournful thing is sad, but not every sad thing is mournful.
What Can Be Described as Mournful?

This word is flexible. It can be used to describe:

A person's expression or eyes:
"She looked at the empty chair with mournful eyes."
Here, the eyes are visibly carrying grief. You can see the sorrow in them.

A person's voice or tone:
"He spoke in a low, mournful voice about his late father."
The sadness is audible — it comes through in how someone speaks.

A sound or piece of music:
"The cello played a mournful melody at the service."
Certain sounds — a slow, low piece of music, a distant cry, the howl of wind — can feel heavy with sorrow.

A cry or wail:
"The child let out a mournful wail when the puppy was taken away."
A mournful cry is not just any cry. It is one that sounds full of grief.

A sigh:
"She gave a long, mournful sigh before putting the letter down."
Even a sigh can be mournful if it carries the weight of deep sadness.

A place or atmosphere:
"The abandoned house had a mournful, forgotten feeling to it."
Places can feel mournful too — old graveyards, empty rooms that were once full of life, or a quiet town after something tragic happened. The sadness is almost in the air.
The Feeling It Creates in the Reader or Listener

When you describe something as mournful, you are telling your reader or listener two things at once:

  1. There is deep sadness here.
  2. That sadness is visible, audible, or felt — it is being expressed outwardly in some way.

It creates a heavy, tender, lingering emotional image. Mournful things do not feel sharp or angry. They feel quiet, slow, and aching — like a wound that still hasn't healed.

Mournful sits at the heavier end of the sadness scale. It is not mild. Consider this rough scale:

Blue → Sad → Sorrowful → Mournful → Devastated

It is more intense than simply "sad" or "unhappy," but it doesn't quite reach the extremes of words like "devastated" or "heartbroken." It lives in the space of deep, grief-filled, quietly expressed sorrow.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

Sorrowful — Very similar to mournful. Both suggest deep sadness. However, "sorrowful" focuses slightly more on the internal feeling, while "mournful" leans slightly more toward the outward expression of that feeling.

Melancholy — A quieter, more reflective sadness that lingers over a long time. Melancholy has a dreamier, more thoughtful quality. Mournful feels heavier and more directly grief-like.

Doleful — Very close to mournful. Both suggest a sad, gloomy expression. They can often be used interchangeably, though "mournful" feels slightly more serious and weighty.

Woeful — Similar, but "woeful" can sometimes be used in more dramatic or even mildly humorous situations ("He had a woeful look on his face after dropping his ice cream"). Mournful is always sincere and never lighthearted.

Forlorn — Suggests sadness combined with a sense of abandonment or hopelessness. A lost dog is forlorn. A crying widow at a graveside is mournful.

These are words that naturally go with "mournful" in everyday use:

  • Mournful eyes
  • Mournful expression / look
  • Mournful voice / tone
  • Mournful cry / wail / howl
  • Mournful song / melody / tune / music
  • Mournful sigh
  • Mournful silence
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Mournful" is a slightly formal and literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in writing — novels, poetry, news articles, or formal descriptions — than in casual, everyday conversation. Someone might say "he looked so sad" in normal speech, but a writer would reach for "mournful" to paint a more precise and evocative picture.

This does not mean you cannot use it in speech — you absolutely can. It simply carries a slightly elevated, expressive quality that makes it especially powerful in writing.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Mournful = deeply and visibly full of grief-like sadness, expressed through someone's eyes, voice, sound, or the feeling of a place.
10923:
Mourning is the experience of deep sadness and sorrow that a person goes through after losing someone or something they loved or valued deeply. It is most commonly associated with the death of a person, but it can apply to any significant loss.

Think of it this way: when something precious is taken away from you permanently, and your heart aches because of that absence — that aching, that sorrow, that process of coming to terms with the loss — that is mourning.

Mourning is not a single moment of sadness. It is a process — something that unfolds over time. It has multiple layers:

The emotional layer — This includes feelings like intense sadness, emptiness, longing, heartache, and sometimes anger, guilt, or disbelief. A person in mourning might cry frequently, feel disconnected from the world, or feel as though a part of themselves is missing.

The behavioral layer — Mourning often shows itself in how a person acts. They might withdraw from social activities, lose interest in things they once enjoyed, talk about the person they lost, or visit places connected to them.

The social and cultural layer — Many societies have specific rituals, traditions, and customs that mark mourning. These include funerals, wearing black clothes, observing a period of silence, lighting candles, and holding memorial services. These practices exist to honor the dead and to give the living a structured way to express their sorrow together.
The Difference Between Mourning, Grief, and Bereavement

These three words are closely related and often used interchangeably, but they are not identical. Understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "mourning."

Grief is the raw, internal emotional pain you feel inside. It is the immediate, often overwhelming wave of sorrow. It is largely private and invisible — what happens inside you.

Bereavement is the state or condition of having suffered a loss, particularly the death of someone close. It is more of a factual status — you are bereaved means you are someone who has recently lost a loved one.

Mourning is the outward expression and ongoing process of working through grief. It is what grief looks like when it is expressed, lived through, and shown — whether privately over a long period or publicly through rituals and customs. While grief is what you feel, mourning is what you do with that feeling over time.

In short: grief is the wound; mourning is the healing journey.

There is no fixed duration. Mourning is deeply personal. Some people mourn intensely for weeks or months and gradually return to everyday life. Others carry a quieter, gentler form of mourning for years — sometimes for a lifetime. It does not mean something is wrong with them. It simply reflects how deeply they loved.

The intensity of mourning usually softens over time. The person learns to live alongside the loss rather than being crushed by it. This is different from forgetting — mourning can coexist with happy memories and even with joy in life.

While death is the most common trigger, mourning can be felt for many kinds of loss:

  • The death of a loved one (most common)
  • The end of a deeply meaningful relationship
  • The loss of one's health or physical ability
  • Losing a home, a homeland, or a way of life
  • The death of a beloved pet
  • The passing of one's youth or a stage of life

In all these cases, the word "mourning" captures that same quality: a deep, sorrowful acknowledgment that something precious is gone and cannot be returned.

• "In mourning" — This means someone is currently going through the mourning process. "She was in mourning for months after her father passed away."
  • "A period of mourning" — A specific stretch of time set aside for mourning, often with cultural or religious guidelines. "The family observed a two-week period of mourning."
  • "National mourning" — When an entire country collectively mourns the loss of a respected leader, a tragedy, or a significant event. "The nation observed three days of national mourning after the disaster."
  • "Mourning the loss of" — A phrase used to describe what specifically is being mourned. "He spent years mourning the loss of his closest friend."

• Her mourning was quiet but deep — she rarely spoke about it, but her eyes told the whole story.
  • The mourning in that household lasted long after the funeral was over.
  • People from across the country joined in mourning when the beloved leader died.
  • His mourning for the life he had left behind was just as real as any other kind of grief.

It is worth noting that mourning is not just sadness — it also carries a sense of dignity and love. To mourn someone is, in a way, to honor them. It is proof that they mattered, that their existence left a mark on your life. Many philosophers and thinkers have pointed out that mourning is one of the most purely human experiences — the price we pay for having loved deeply.

Mourning (noun) is the deep sorrow and the outward, ongoing process of coping with a significant loss — most often the death of someone loved. It involves emotional pain, behavioral changes, and often cultural or social rituals. It differs from grief (which is the internal feeling) and bereavement (which is the condition of having lost someone). Mourning takes time, varies in length from person to person, and is ultimately a reflection of love and attachment.
10924:
A moustache is the hair that grows on a person's upper lip — the area sitting right between the bottom of the nose and the top of the mouth. It is a type of facial hair, and it refers only to that specific strip of hair on the upper lip. Nothing more, nothing less.

It is important to know what a moustache is not, so you don't confuse it with related words:

  • Beard — hair growing on the chin, jaw, and cheeks. Not the upper lip.
  • Stubble — very short, rough facial hair all over the face, usually from not shaving for a few days.
  • Sideburns — strips of hair growing on the sides of the face, along the cheeks in front of the ears.

A person can have a moustache without a beard, or a beard without a moustache, or both together.

While any human being can grow facial hair given the right hormonal conditions, a moustache is almost always associated with men, since male hormones (especially testosterone) promote facial hair growth. Some women, particularly after certain hormonal changes in life, may develop faint hair on the upper lip too, but this is generally not called a moustache in everyday conversation.

You may see this word spelled in two ways:

  • Moustache — used in British English (UK, Australia, India, and most of the world)
  • Mustache — used in American English (USA)

Both spellings refer to the exact same thing. Neither is wrong — it simply depends on which variety of English you are reading or writing.
What It Looks Like — Styles and Shapes

A moustache is not always the same. People grow and groom them in many different ways, and over the centuries, various distinct styles have become recognizable enough to have their own names. Here are some of the most well-known:

  • Pencil moustache — extremely thin and narrow, carefully trimmed to a neat line just above the lip. It looks almost drawn on.
  • Chevron moustache — thick, wide, and full, neatly sitting across the upper lip. A very classic, tidy style.
  • Handlebar moustache — long at the sides, with the ends curled or twisted upward, resembling the handlebars of a bicycle.
  • Walrus moustache — very thick and bushy, drooping downward over the upper lip and sometimes covering the mouth partially.
  • Horseshoe moustache — shaped like an upside-down U (or a horseshoe), with lines of hair running from the upper lip straight down past the corners of the mouth toward the chin.
  • Fu Manchu moustache — similar to the horseshoe, but the downward strips grow very long and thin, hanging well below the chin.
  • Imperial moustache — a large, dramatic moustache with the ends curled or swept dramatically upward.

In everyday life, most people simply have a "moustache" without labeling the style. These specific style names are used when you want to be more precise.

While a moustache almost always refers to actual facial hair, the word is sometimes used playfully or figuratively:

  • Milk moustache — when someone drinks milk and a white residue is left on their upper lip, people humorously call it a "milk moustache." This is not real hair, of course, but the shape and location are the same.
  • In art and humor, drawing a moustache on a portrait or photograph (such as adding one to the Mona Lisa) is a classic joke or act of parody. The moustache here is symbolic — it is placed on the upper lip of the painted face.

The moustache carries meaning beyond just appearance:

  • Historically, moustaches have been associated with masculinity, authority, and maturity in many cultures around the world.
  • In some cultures and historical periods, military officers and figures of authority were expected to wear moustaches.
  • Movember is a globally recognized annual event held in November, during which men grow moustaches to raise awareness for men's health issues such as prostate cancer and mental health. The word "Movember" itself combines "mo" (an informal word for moustache, especially in Australian and British slang) with "November."
  • The moustache has also been strongly associated with specific famous figures throughout history — so much so that a certain style of moustache can immediately remind people of a historical person.

These are natural word pairings you will often encounter:

  • Grow a moustache — to let the hair on the upper lip develop over time
  • Shave off a moustache — to remove it with a razor
  • Trim a moustache — to cut and tidy it without fully removing it
  • Sport a moustache — a slightly formal or literary way to say someone has a moustache ("He sported a thick, grey moustache.")
  • Twirl a moustache — to twist the ends with one's fingers; this phrase is also used figuratively to describe a cartoonishly villainous character
  • A thick/thin/bushy/neat/trim/well-groomed moustache — common adjectives used to describe it

Here are some sentences showing how the word is naturally used:

  1. He decided to grow a moustache after seeing an old photograph of his grandfather.
  2. The detective had a neat, pencil-thin moustache that made him look sharp and precise.
  3. She noticed he had shaved off his moustache and almost didn't recognize him.
  4. The villain in the old film would constantly twirl his long, curled moustache.
  5. After drinking his hot chocolate too quickly, he ended up with a foamy moustache above his lip.
  6. The soldier wore a thick walrus moustache that had turned grey with age.

A moustache is simply the hair on a person's upper lip. It is a specific type of facial hair with a specific location on the face. It can be short or long, thick or thin, neat or wild — and it can carry cultural, historical, or personal significance. Whenever you see or hear the word, that is all it means: hair, upper lip.
10925: The word "mousy" draws everything it means from one simple image: a mouse. Think of a mouse — small, grey, timid, quiet, and easy to overlook. "Mousy" takes those qualities and applies them to either a color or a person. It has three related meanings, all rooted in that same image.

When "mousy" describes a color, it means a flat, dull, brownish-grey shade — exactly the color of a mouse's fur. This usage is almost always applied to hair.

"Mousy hair" is not blonde, not a rich chestnut brown, not any vibrant or striking shade. It sits in an unremarkable in-between zone — a washed-out, lifeless brownish-grey that doesn't catch the eye. The word quietly implies that this color is plain and forgettable.

"She had mousy brown hair she always kept pinned up."
"After she stopped dyeing it, her natural mousy color started showing at the roots."
Meaning 2: Timid, Shy, and Unassertive (the most common meaning)

When "mousy" describes a person, it means someone who is quiet, meek, timid, and lacking in confidence — someone who, much like a mouse, tends to stay in the background, avoid drawing attention, and shrink away from confrontation.

A mousy person:

  • speaks very softly, hesitantly, or barely at all
  • avoids asserting themselves, even when they should
  • lets others speak over them or ignore them without objecting
  • seems nervous, cautious, or easily intimidated in social situations
  • blends into a room rather than standing out in it

Picture a mouse hugging the wall, darting around quietly, avoiding being noticed. A mousy person behaves the same way in the human world — they don't speak up in meetings, they don't push back when treated unfairly, they don't command a room. They go unnoticed.

"The new intern was so mousy that people kept forgetting she was in the room."
"He was a mousy, soft-spoken man who agreed with everyone."
"She used to be mousy and nervous, but after a few years she became far more confident."
Meaning 3: Having the Smell Associated with Mice

Less commonly, "mousy" can describe a smell — the stale, musty, slightly unpleasant odor that mice leave behind in spaces they inhabit. You might hear this when describing an old, neglected room or building.

"The storage room had a mousy smell that made her wrinkle her nose."

This meaning is much rarer than the other two, but good to know.
When the Two Main Meanings Combine

Sometimes "mousy" captures both the color and the personality at once, painting a full picture of a person who is plain in appearance and timid in manner — someone thoroughly forgettable in every way. Dull hair, unremarkable features, quiet voice, no confidence. The kind of person who could walk in and out of a room without anyone registering their presence.

"Mousy" is never a compliment. It carries a quietly dismissive, mildly negative feeling. Using it suggests the person or thing being described lacks vitality, boldness, or presence — qualities people generally admire. It can carry a hint of pity ("the poor mousy little thing") or mild contempt, depending on context.

Importantly, it is rarely said to someone's face. It's the kind of word used in descriptions, narration, or conversation about someone — not to them.

A small but useful distinction: "mouse-like" is a neutral, purely factual comparison — it just means resembling a mouse in some way. "Mousy" goes further — it carries a judgment. It implies that resembling a mouse in this way is a shortcoming.

ColorDull, flat, brownish-grey (usually hair)
PersonalityTimid, quiet, unassertive, lacking presence
SmellMusty, stale, mouse-like odor (rare)
ToneMildly negative; not a compliment
10926:
Before diving into the individual meanings, understand this one central idea that ties everything together:

A mouthpiece is something — either a physical object or a person — that acts as the outlet or channel through which sound, breath, or a message travels outward.

Think of it like a funnel. Whatever needs to come out — air, music, words, opinions — the mouthpiece is the thing it comes out through. Keep this image in mind as you read each meaning below, and everything will click into place.
Meaning 1: A Physical Part of an Object (The Most Literal Meaning)

This is the simplest meaning. A mouthpiece is the part of an object that you put in or near your mouth to use it.

Here are the most common examples:

  • Musical instruments — A trumpet, trombone, or tuba has a small cup-shaped piece at one end. You press your lips against it and blow. That piece is the mouthpiece. Without it, you can't play the instrument. A clarinet or saxophone has a slightly different kind — you put it between your lips. Same idea, same name.
  • A pipe — Whether it's a tobacco pipe or any other kind, the narrow end that you put in your mouth to draw smoke or air through is the mouthpiece.
  • A telephone or microphone — The part you speak into — the part you hold close to your mouth — is the mouthpiece. (The earpiece, by contrast, is what you hold to your ear to listen.) On older phones, this distinction was very clear.
  • Breathing equipment — In scuba diving gear or a gas mask, the rubber piece you bite down on or place in your mouth to breathe through is the mouthpiece.

The pattern: In all these cases, the mouthpiece is the critical physical point where your mouth meets the object, and where something (air, sound, breath, words) passes through and goes outward.

In boxing, martial arts, rugby, and other contact sports, athletes wear a soft rubber or plastic guard inside their mouth to protect their teeth and jaw from blows. This is called a mouthpiece (also called a mouth guard).

It sits in the mouth, hence the name. Simple and direct.
Meaning 3: A Person Who Speaks on Behalf of Someone Else (Very Important Meaning)

This is where the word becomes more powerful and interesting. A mouthpiece can be a person whose job — or role — is to say things publicly on behalf of another person, group, organization, or government.

Think about it this way: just as a trumpet's mouthpiece channels the musician's breath and turns it into music that the world hears, a human mouthpiece channels someone else's thoughts and delivers them to the public.

Example: A government spokesperson who stands in front of cameras and reads official statements is acting as the government's mouthpiece. The words coming out of their mouth are not necessarily their own personal views — they are the government's views, delivered through this person.

Crucial nuance — the tone of this word:
When you call someone a mouthpiece, you are usually being slightly critical or neutral-to-negative, not complimentary. The word subtly suggests that the person is not thinking independently. They are simply repeating and delivering what someone more powerful tells them to say — like a puppet whose strings are being pulled. They are a vessel for someone else's message, not an original voice.

You would not typically call a bold, independent journalist who speaks their own mind a "mouthpiece." But you might call a loyalist party spokesperson, or a commentator who always defends a powerful figure without question, a mouthpiece.

More examples of this usage:

  • "That news anchor is just a mouthpiece for the government." (meaning: they only repeat official positions and don't challenge them)
  • "The CEO used his assistant as a mouthpiece to avoid speaking to the press directly."
Meaning 4: A Publication or Media Outlet That Represents a Group's Views

Extending the same idea, an entire newspaper, TV channel, website, or publication can be called a mouthpiece if it consistently and reliably promotes the views of a specific group, political party, organization, or ideology.

Example: "That newspaper is widely considered a mouthpiece of the ruling party" — meaning the newspaper doesn't independently report the news; it serves as a vehicle to spread that party's message and agenda.

Again, the word carries a critical or skeptical tone here. Calling a publication a mouthpiece implies it lacks independence and objectivity.

In informal, colloquial English — especially in American English and especially in older films, crime novels, or street language — a mouthpiece means a lawyer, particularly a defense attorney.

The logic is vivid: a lawyer is literally the person who speaks for you in court. They are your voice in front of a judge. Your words come out through their mouth.

Example: "He was in trouble with the law and called his mouthpiece right away." (meaning: he called his lawyer)

This usage is somewhat old-fashioned today, but you will still encounter it in books, movies, and everyday speech, so it's worth knowing.

Here is a quick mental map of all the meanings under one roof:

SituationWhat "mouthpiece" refers to
Playing a trumpetThe metal cup you press your lips to
Using an old telephoneThe part you speak into
Boxing matchThe rubber guard protecting your teeth
A government press secretaryA person who delivers official messages on behalf of those in power
A state-controlled newspaperA publication that promotes one group's agenda
Courtroom slangA defense lawyer

No matter which meaning you encounter, the underlying thread is always the same: something or someone through which a message, sound, or breath flows outward on behalf of something else. Master that concept, and you will understand "mouthpiece" in every context you ever see it.
10927:
When someone says they will "move heaven and earth" to do something, it means they will try absolutely everything in their power to make it happen. They will spare no effort, give up no obstacle, and stop at nothing to succeed.

Think of it this way: Heaven and Earth are the two largest things imaginable — the sky above and the ground below. If a person were somehow able to physically move both of them, that would require an almost impossible, superhuman level of effort. So when someone says "I will move heaven and earth," they are using those giant images to express that their effort will be just as extreme and unstoppable.

In short, it means: "I will do everything possible, no matter how hard."
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Even though the phrase sounds literal, it is completely figurative — nobody is actually moving the sky or the ground. This kind of exaggeration used to make a point stronger is called a hyperbole (pronounced hy-PER-boh-lee). It's the same kind of exaggeration you use when you say "I've told you a million times" — you don't mean exactly one million; you just mean "many times."

So in "move heaven and earth," the exaggeration is used to say: "My effort will be so huge, it's like moving the entire universe."

This idiom is very old. A similar expression appeared in the writings of the ancient Greek orator Demosthenes (around 384–322 BC). He used a phrase that meant using every possible force — both the divine (heaven) and the earthly (earth) — to get something done.

The expression later found its way into English literature and everyday speech, and over centuries it became the fixed phrase we know today: "move heaven and earth."

Because it uses "heaven" and "earth," it reflects the old worldview where everything that existed fell into one of two categories: the heavenly realm above, and the earthly world below. Together, they represented everything that exists. So to move both of them means to mobilize everything that exists in service of your goal.
How to Use It — Grammar and Structure

This idiom almost always follows a specific pattern:

[Subject] + will/would + move heaven and earth + to + [achieve something]

Here are some examples:

  • "She will move heaven and earth to make sure her son gets the best medical treatment."
  • "He moved heaven and earth to get the project completed before the deadline."
  • "I would move heaven and earth to protect my family."
  • "The rescue team moved heaven and earth to find the missing hikers."

Notice that it works in different tenses — you can say will move (future), moved (past), or would move (conditional). The core phrase "move heaven and earth" stays the same.
What Kind of Situations Is It Used For?

This idiom is used when the goal being pursued is genuinely important — something the person cares deeply about. You would not normally say "I'll move heaven and earth to find my missing pen," because that's too small and trivial. The idiom carries weight, so it fits situations like:

  • Protecting a loved one
  • Fighting for justice
  • Achieving a lifelong dream
  • Solving a serious crisis
  • Getting someone the help they desperately need

Using it for a very minor goal would sound strange or even funny.
The Feeling Behind It — Tone and Emotion

This idiom carries a tone of deep commitment, fierce determination, and emotional intensity. When a person says it, they want you to feel the full force of their dedication. It's a strong, passionate statement — not casual.

You can use it:

  • About yourself: "I will move heaven and earth to give my kids a better life."
  • About someone else: "She moved heaven and earth to clear her brother's name."

It works in both spoken and written English, and fits both formal and informal situations.

To avoid confusion, here is what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean something is impossible — quite the opposite. It means the person is saying they will succeed no matter what.
  • It does not involve anything supernatural or magical. It's purely about human effort and determination.
  • It does not mean a person is being reckless or careless — it just means they are being maximally determined.
Similar Idioms (In Case You Encounter Them)

Other English idioms carry a similar meaning of "doing everything possible":

  • "Leave no stone unturned" — try every possible option
  • "Go to the ends of the earth" — travel anywhere, do anything to achieve a goal
  • "Pull out all the stops" — use every available resource or strategy
  • "Do everything in one's power" — a more literal, less dramatic way to say the same thing
  • "Bend over backwards" — make a very big effort, often for someone else's benefit

All of these express great effort or determination, but "move heaven and earth" is among the most dramatic and emotionally powerful of them all.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

MeaningTo do absolutely everything possible to achieve a goal
TypeIdiom (specifically, a hyperbole)
ToneStrong, determined, emotional
Used forImportant, serious goals — not trivial things
Key grammarSubject + will/would/moved + heaven and earth + to + goal
Example"She will move heaven and earth to find her missing daughter."

The beauty of this idiom is in its imagery. The moment you hear it, you get a vivid mental picture of someone straining to move the sky and the ground — and that image immediately tells you: this person is not giving up, no matter what.
10928:
When someone says they can "move mountains", they mean they can achieve something that seems completely impossible through sheer determination, effort, or strong belief. Literally moving a mountain is physically impossible for a human being — and that is exactly the point. The idiom uses this impossibility to express an idea of extraordinary power, will, or effort.

It is also used to describe going to extreme lengths to help someone or to get something done — even if it costs tremendous effort or sacrifice.

Think of it this way: if someone loves you so much that they would "move mountains" for you, it means there is almost nothing they wouldn't do to help or support you.

This idiom carries two slightly different but related meanings depending on how it is used:

1. To accomplish the seemingly impossible through great effort or determination.
This means working so hard, or being so determined, that you are able to overcome obstacles that would stop most other people.

2. To do whatever it takes — no matter how difficult — for someone or something.
This focuses more on willingness and devotion. It says: "I care so much that I would tackle even the most impossible challenge for you."

Both meanings are about extraordinary human will going far beyond what is considered normal or easy.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

This idiom has ancient roots and comes primarily from the Bible, which is why it has been around for thousands of years and is understood in many languages and cultures.

In the Bible, specifically in Matthew 17:20, Jesus tells his disciples:

"If you have faith as small as a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you."

And in 1 Corinthians 13:2, the apostle Paul writes:

"If I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing."

In both of these passages, moving a mountain is used as the ultimate symbol of impossible achievement — something only possible through immense faith or love. Over centuries, this image worked its way from religious texts into everyday language, and today you don't have to be religious at all to use the idiom. It simply became a universal metaphor for overcoming the impossible.
How Is It Used in Sentences?

Here are several example sentences across different contexts so you can see the idiom in action:

Describing personal determination:
"She studied day and night and moved mountains to pass that exam."
(She worked incredibly hard to achieve something very difficult.)

Describing love or devotion:
"He would move mountains for his children."
(He would do absolutely anything — no matter how hard — for his children.)

Describing teamwork or collective effort:
"When this team works together, they can move mountains."
(Together, they can accomplish things that seem impossible.)

Describing faith or belief:
"Her belief in herself moved mountains — she started with nothing and built a successful company."
(Her self-belief allowed her to achieve what others thought was impossible.)

Describing someone helping another person:
"My mentor moved mountains to get me an internship at that company."
(My mentor made extraordinary efforts on my behalf.)
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom is always positive and admiring in tone. When you use it, you are expressing:

  • Deep admiration for someone's effort or strength
  • A sense of awe at what has been or can be achieved
  • Warmth and devotion when talking about helping someone

It is never used sarcastically in its standard form. If someone moved mountains, they deserve respect and recognition.
What This Idiom Is NOT Saying

It is important to understand what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean someone is literally going to dig up a mountain.
  • It does not refer to small or ordinary tasks. You would never say "She moved mountains to make breakfast." That would sound odd and exaggerated. The idiom is reserved for genuinely difficult, significant challenges.
  • It does not imply luck. Moving mountains is always about deliberate effort, will, faith, or love — never about being in the right place at the right time.

You will encounter this idiom in several slightly different forms, but the core meaning stays the same:

  • "Move mountains" — the base idiom. "She can move mountains."
  • "Faith can move mountains" — emphasizing belief as the driving force.
  • "Would move mountains for someone" — emphasizing devotion and willingness to help.
  • "Moved mountains to do something" — referring to something already accomplished through great effort.
A Simple Way to Always Remember It

Here is an easy mental trick: Picture a mountain. Now imagine a single human being pushing it and actually moving it. That is physically impossible, right? Now apply that feeling of impossibility to a life situation — a goal so hard it seems impossible. "Moving mountains" means achieving exactly that — the impossible — through will, faith, love, or effort.

ConceptDetail

The idiom "move mountains" means to achieve something seemingly impossible, or to go to extraordinary lengths for someone or something. It comes from the Bible, where moving a mountain symbolised the ultimate act of faith. Today, it is used to express intense determination, deep love, or remarkable effort. It is always positive in tone and is only used for genuinely great challenges — never trivial ones.
10929:
To understand this idiom, picture a football match. The goalposts are fixed structures at each end of the field. A player's entire goal is to kick the ball between those posts. Now imagine that just as a player is about to score, someone secretly moves the posts further away. The player runs the same distance, puts in the same effort, and kicks just as hard — but suddenly it's not good enough anymore. The target has changed, and nobody warned them.

That visual image is the soul of this idiom.

"Move the goalposts" means to unfairly change the rules, requirements, or conditions of something after someone has already started working toward the original goal.

The key word here is unfairly. This idiom always carries a sense of injustice or dishonesty. The person whose goalposts get moved feels cheated — they did exactly what was asked, but the other side quietly changed what "success" looks like, making it harder or even impossible to win.
The Three Core Ideas Inside This Idiom

Understanding these three ideas will lock the meaning in your mind permanently:

1. There was an original, agreed-upon target.
Before the goalposts move, both sides understand what "done" or "success" looks like. There's a clear standard everyone accepts.

2. Someone changes that target mid-way.
While one person is working hard toward the original goal, the other person shifts the conditions — often quietly, often without warning, and almost always to their own advantage.

3. The change is unfair and one-sided.
This is not a mutual renegotiation where both sides sit down and agree to new terms. It's a unilateral, sneaky shift. The person doing it holds more power in the situation.

This idiom shows up in almost every area of life:

At work:
Your boss tells you that if you hit a sales target of $50,000 this month, you'll get a bonus. You work incredibly hard and hit $50,000. Then your boss says, "Actually, I meant $70,000." That's moving the goalposts.

In a relationship:
Your partner says they'll be happy if you spend more weekends at home. You start doing exactly that. Then they say they also need you to call more during the week, and then they add more conditions. Every time you meet one expectation, a new one appears. That's moving the goalposts.

In politics:
A government promises to approve a community's housing project if they meet three specific conditions. The community meets all three. The government then invents two new conditions. Politicians and journalists use this idiom constantly.

In a negotiation:
A buyer says they'll purchase your car for $10,000 if you fix the tyres. You fix the tyres and spend money doing so. They then say they also need the engine checked before they'll pay. That's moving the goalposts.

In academics:
A professor tells a student their thesis will pass if they add one more chapter. The student adds it. The professor then says the introduction also needs to be rewritten. And then the conclusion. The original requirement keeps expanding. That's moving the goalposts.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom is almost always negative and accusatory. When someone says "you're moving the goalposts," they are:

  • Calling out unfair behavior
  • Expressing frustration or anger
  • Accusing the other person of acting in bad faith
  • Refusing to be manipulated further

It is rarely used in a neutral way. If you hear someone say it, there is almost certainly conflict or tension in the situation.

This idiom is widely used in:

  • Everyday English conversation — especially in arguments or complaints
  • Business and management — when deadlines, targets, or deliverables keep changing
  • Politics and journalism — one of the most common idioms in political reporting
  • Law and negotiation — when terms of an agreement are altered unfairly

It is common in both British English and American English, though it originated in British usage (where "football" means soccer, and goalposts are a vivid part of the culture).
How to Use It in a Sentence

The most natural constructions are:

  • "They keep moving the goalposts." (general frustration)
  • "Stop moving the goalposts." (a direct accusation or plea)
  • "The goalposts have been moved." (describing what happened, in a more formal tone)
  • "Every time I get close, they move the goalposts." (expressing repeated frustration)
  • "This feels like moving the goalposts." (a softer, more diplomatic way to raise the concern)

It's important to separate this idiom from situations that look similar but aren't quite the same:

  • If both parties mutually agree to change a goal, that is a renegotiation, not moving the goalposts.
  • If new external circumstances genuinely force a change (like a natural disaster or a law change), that is not really moving the goalposts either — there is no bad faith involved.
  • If someone clarifies what they meant from the beginning (and the original goal was genuinely unclear), that is also not quite moving the goalposts.

The idiom specifically requires intentional unfairness on someone's part. The bad faith element is what makes it "moving the goalposts" rather than just "changing plans."

A closely related expression is "changing the rules mid-game" — it carries the same spirit. You might also hear "shifting the goalposts," which means exactly the same thing as "moving the goalposts." These are interchangeable.

"Move the goalposts" = unfairly changing what someone needs to do to succeed, after they've already started working toward the original goal.

If you remember the image of a football player sprinting toward a goal only to find the posts have been secretly dragged further away — you will never forget this idiom.
